strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem formulation: the paper is among the first to explicitly frame concept drift (changing anomaly definitions) in VAD and to formalize language-conditioned detection as learning a mapping (v,z)->y, which is a meaningful paradigm shift beyond open-set/open-vocabulary VAD.

Substantial dataset contribution: PreVAD (35,279 videos) is significantly larger and more diverse than prior VAD datasets, with a hierarchical taxonomy and fine-grained anomaly descriptions; the multi-stage foundation-model-assisted curation pipeline is a practical contribution toward reducing annotation cost.

Comprehensive and mostly fair evaluation: zero-shot comparison across seven datasets with reproduced baselines (PEL, VadCLIP) using public weights, plus a new classification protocol covering both normal and abnormal videos; a 20% AP gain on XD-Violence and consistent SOTA across datasets is convincing.

Good ablation design: the paper disentangles dataset effect from architecture effect by training VadCLIP on PreVAD (13.6% avg gain) versus LaGoVAD on identical data (7.2% gain), supporting the claim that both the data and the language-conditioned design contribute; module ablations and concept-drift qualitative visualizations further substantiate the paradigm.
Data and code release is promised, and the benchmark setup (cross-dataset zero-shot evaluation on seven datasets) is a useful community resource.
weaknesses: Potential train-test contamination is not convincingly addressed: PreVAD is sourced from web videos and existing video-text datasets, the same sources as many of the seven zero-shot test datasets (e.g., UCF-Crime, XD-Violence also come from web/movie sources). No deduplication or overlap analysis against the test sets is reported, which is critical for the validity of the zero-shot claims.

The annotation quality of PreVAD relies heavily on MLLM/VLM/LLM-generated descriptions with only hybrid human verification, and no test set is manually annotated; the actual noise level of labels and descriptions is not quantified, weakening claims about dataset quality.

Technical novelty of the model components is moderate: dynamic video synthesis is essentially feature-level Mosaic/Cutout-style augmentation, and the contrastive loss with hard negative mining is a fairly standard formulation; neither involves deep methodological novelty, and the loss equations (Sec. 4.1) are confusingly written with key details deferred to supplementary material.

Absolute zero-shot classification performance remains weak (e.g., 51.7% accuracy on UCF-Crime), suggesting the language-guided mechanism is far from a solved problem; the paper could be more candid about this limitation.

No variance/significance reporting over multiple runs, and some important details (retrieval metrics for synthesis, hyperparameters, prompt design) are deferred to the appendix, limiting immediate reproducibility.

The claim that conditioning on language 'avoids' concept drift is somewhat overstated: the paradigm shifts the drift to the definition input, and success depends on the model faithfully interpreting arbitrary user definitions, which is only demonstrated on limited, hand-picked qualitative examples and a small set of category-name prompts.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and underexplored problem: the anomaly definition can change at test time (concept drift), and conditioning detection on user-provided language is a sensible remedy.

The proposed PreVAD dataset is a substantial resource contribution (35,279 videos with hierarchical taxonomy and anomaly descriptions), and the automated curation pipeline is well motivated for scalability.

Evaluation breadth is above average for the area: zero-shot detection on seven datasets plus zero-shot classification, with reproduced baselines (PEL, VadCLIP) under the same CLIP variant, and controlled comparisons of VadCLIP trained on PreVAD vs. UCF/XD to isolate dataset effects.
Ablations cover each regularization module and the effect of removing language guidance, and the qualitative concept-drift examples (Fig. 7) directly illustrate the claimed capability.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the proposed paradigm is essentially language/open-vocabulary-conditioned VAD. OVVAD [34] and VadCLIP [35] already condition on text; the main delta is framing label change as 'concept drift' and adding two regularization losses (a Mosaic/Cutout-style video concatenation and a standard contrastive loss with hard negatives). The theoretical treatment (Eqs. 1-4) is a reformulation rather than a substantive analysis, and the 'stochastic variable' modeling of z is not actually realized as anything stochastic in the method.

Potential train-test contamination undermines the central zero-shot claims: PreVAD is collected from web videos and existing video-text datasets, and the zero-shot test sets (UCF-Crime, XD-Violence, LAD, TAD, DoTA, MSAD) are also web-sourced. The paper reports no near-duplicate de-duplication or overlap check between PreVAD and the evaluation sets, so the large reported gains could partly reflect memorization rather than open-world generalization. This must be addressed for the SOTA claim to be credible.

Annotation quality is unverified: the fine-grained anomaly descriptions are generated by an MLLM under constrained prompts with only weak hybrid human oversight, and no human evaluation of description accuracy/label noise is reported. Since descriptions are a core training signal for the language-conditioned mapping, noisy auto-annotations are a significant soundness concern.

The 'user-defined anomaly at inference' capability is evaluated narrowly: zero-shot evaluation uses manually designed prompts based on each dataset's fixed class names, which is close to the closed category sets of prior work. There is no systematic study of free-form, user-authored definitions (e.g., sensitivity to phrasing, compositional definitions, unseen categories), so the open-world claim is demonstrated mainly through two cherry-picked qualitative cases.

Fairness of comparisons: LaGoVAD is trained on 35K videos versus baselines trained on 1.9K-5K; the controlled VadCLIP-on-PreVAD comparison helps, but the headline gains in Fig. 2 conflate dataset scale with paradigm advantage, and the comparison against LAVAD [40] (training-free) does not control for the use of large pretrained models.

Presentation issues reduce clarity: Table 4 is difficult to parse (checkmark rows vs. the 'PreVAD' column semantics are unclear); the claimed '20% improvement on XD-Violence' and '68% improvement in classification accuracy' need more precise baselines; several key details (synthesis module specifics, negative mining implementation, prompts) are deferred to supplementary material that is not provided for review.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely underexplored and practically important problem: concept drift in VAD, where the definition of 'anomaly' changes across deployment scenarios and user requirements. The proposed language-guided paradigm (conditioning predictions on both video v and definition z) is a sensible and clearly motivated reformulation.

PreVAD is a substantial resource contribution: at 35,279 videos with multi-level taxonomy and anomaly descriptions, it is by far the largest VAD dataset with text annotations, and the automated curation pipeline (MLLM description generation + VLM/LLM verification) is a scalable design.

Empirical evaluation is broad and reasonably convincing: zero-shot detection across seven diverse datasets with consistent SOTA results (e.g., 20% improvement on XD-Violence), plus fair re-training of strong baselines (VadCLIP, PEL) on identical data to disentangle dataset vs. architecture effects.

Ablation studies (Tab. 4) cleanly isolate the contributions of dynamic video synthesis, contrastive loss with hard negative mining, and language guidance, and the qualitative concept-drift examples in Fig. 7 directly illustrate the claimed capability that prior methods lack.
The writing and figures (paradigm comparison, dataset statistics, architecture) are clear and well organized, and the paper commits to releasing data and code.
weaknesses: The core model design is technically incremental: a CLIP-based two-branch detector with standard MIL losses, contrastive learning with hard negative mining, and Mosaic/Cutout-style video stitching. The individual techniques are well-executed but not novel; the contribution rests heavily on the problem framing and the dataset.

The relationship to open-vocabulary VAD (OVVAD [34]) deserves sharper delineation. Open-vocabulary methods already condition detection on text at inference; the paper's conceptual novelty is the 'label alteration' argument, but this is quantitatively tested only via two qualitative examples (Fig. 7). A controlled benchmark specifically measuring adaptation to redefined anomaly labels would substantially strengthen the central claim.

Data contamination risk is not addressed: PreVAD is web-collected while most test datasets (UCF-Crime, XD-Violence, DoTA, etc.) are also web-sourced. No deduplication or overlap analysis is reported, which is important for validating true zero-shot generalization.

PreVAD labels and descriptions are generated by foundation models (MLLM/VLM/LLM) with hybrid human-AI annotation, but no label-noise statistics or human verification rates are provided. The lack of a held-out test set makes it difficult to assess dataset quality independently.

The theoretical framing is relatively thin: Eq. (2) relies on the assumption that Y is determined solely by (V, Z), so 'avoiding concept drift' is essentially by construction; the factorization does not clearly explain why training on diverse (v,z,y) triples yields the claimed robustness, and the 'exponentially decaying sample density' argument for overfitting is informal.

Some comparisons are incomplete: the LLM-based training-free method (LAVAD) is only evaluated on UCF/XD, and evaluation on synthetic datasets (UBNormal) and domain-specific datasets (DoTA) mixes very different anomaly definitions into a single average, which may obscure per-domain behavior.

Ethical considerations around large-scale web-scraped surveillance content, privacy of identifiable individuals, and copyright are acknowledged only briefly; given the dataset's scale and release plans, a more thorough treatment is warranted.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation: the paper identifies concept drift (changing anomaly definitions at test time) as a real gap in existing VAD paradigms and formally casts open-world VAD as learning a mapping conditioned on both video and user-provided definition, which is a genuine novelty in this subfield.

Significant dataset contribution: PreVAD (35,279 videos, 209.5 hours) is claimed to be the largest and most diverse VAD dataset with multi-level taxonomy and anomaly descriptions; the curation pipeline is well documented (sources, cleansing with MLLM/LLM verification, hybrid human-AI annotation) and is reproducible at low cost.

Comprehensive evaluation: two zero-shot protocols across seven diverse test datasets, comparisons against weakly-supervised, open-vocabulary, multi-domain, and LLM-based baselines (many reproduced from open-source code under a consistent feature setup), plus a dedicated concept-drift evaluation (drift@5) that directly probes the central claim.

Important controlled comparison included: VadCLIP retrained on PreVAD isolates dataset vs. architecture effects, showing most of the gain comes from the data while the proposed model still adds consistent improvements (7.2% avg detection).

Detailed ablations (component-level, hyperparameters of dynamic video synthesis, prompt types, data usage), qualitative visualizations under concept drift, and sufficient implementation details (single RTX4090, all hyperparameters) supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The theoretical framing is thin: conditioning predictions on Z (Eq. 4) reparameterizes concept drift rather than 'avoiding' it; the formalism (Eqs. 1-2) is informal and the overfitting argument ('exponentially decaying sample density') is asserted rather than demonstrated.

The model components are relatively standard (CLIP features, co-attention fusion, MIL losses, InfoNCE-style contrastive loss with hard negatives); the main technical novelty beyond the task formulation and dataset is limited.

Baseline comparisons are not fully apples-to-apples: LaGoVAD is trained on the much larger PreVAD while most baselines use UCF/XD; although VadCLIP-on-PreVAD mitigates this, several headline comparisons (e.g., 20%/32% improvements on XD) partly conflate data scale with method contribution.

Test-time prompts are manually designed per dataset/class; the prompt ablation shows sensitivity (80.44 vs 81.12 vs 83.03), raising concerns about mild test-set-specific tuning, and no automatic prompt-selection protocol is provided.

Annotation quality relies heavily on MLLM/LLM outputs (descriptions, abnormality judgments) with human verification only for category labels and the validation set; no quantitative inter-annotator agreement or estimated label noise rate for descriptions is reported.

Dynamic video synthesis only concatenates retrieved segments, which is a crude approximation of realistic anomaly duration distributions; potential train/test artifacts from splicing are not analyzed.

Some results are unconvincing or inconsistent: classification F1 on UCF-Crime is very low (16.64) and the component ablation shows removing Lneg barely changes detection (69.87 vs 69.98) while classification degrades sharply, which is not well explained; writing contains multiple typos and inconsistencies (e.g., 'released a', 'protocals').

strengths: The paper identifies a genuinely interesting and underexplored problem: concept drift (changing anomaly definitions) in video anomaly detection, and the motivation with concrete examples (e.g., 'pedestrian on road' being normal vs. abnormal across scenarios) is well argued.

PreVAD is a large-scale contribution: 35,279 videos with a multi-level taxonomy and anomaly descriptions, collected via a documented and mostly reproducible curation pipeline (sources, prompts, and filtering criteria are provided in the appendix).

The evaluation is broad in scope: zero-shot testing across seven diverse datasets, a dedicated drift@5 protocol, ablations of both model components and dataset contributions, and reproduction of most baselines with open-source weights rather than only citing numbers.
Implementation details (hyperparameters, architecture, hardware) are given at a level that supports reproducibility, and a thorough ablation of the synthesis hyperparameters is included.
weaknesses: The formal contribution is thin. Eq. (2) is simply the law of total probability, and conditioning detection on a text input Z is essentially what CLIP-based VAD methods (VadCLIP, OVVAD) already do. The claimed theoretical resolution of concept drift ('we effectively avoid concept drift') is overstated: there is no guarantee the model generalizes to arbitrary user definitions at test time, and no analysis of failure modes when the test definition distribution departs from training definitions.

Comparisons are confounded by training-data scale. LaGoVAD is trained on PreVAD (35K videos, 209.5 hours) while most baselines are trained on UCF-Crime or XD-Violence, orders of magnitude smaller. Although VadCLIP is retrained on PreVAD as a partial control, the headline SOTA claims conflate dataset scale with method novelty, and the model-vs-data attribution is only partially disentangled.

Results are mixed rather than consistently superior: e.g., UCF-Crime classification F1 (16.64) is below VadCLIP's 17.81, and several per-dataset gaps are small relative to noise. No variance/significance reporting is provided for the drift@5 protocol, which relies on only five hand-picked category subsets on just two test sets (XD-Violence, MSAD) — a narrow basis for the central concept-drift claim.

Dataset quality controls are under-verified. Anomaly descriptions are MLLM-generated with limited human oversight; no inter-annotator agreement, hallucination rate, or description-accuracy statistics are reported. For a paper whose core premise is that fine-grained definitions drive detection, the reliability of these definitions is not established. The dynamic video synthesis module also concatenates retrieved clips, which produces temporally incoherent pseudo-videos whose realism/impact is not analyzed.

Comparison methodology with LLM-based baselines is arguably unfair: Qwen2-VL's frame-level scores are binarized from sparse boundary predictions, which mechanically depresses AUC/AP, and the efficiency comparison ('minutes vs. hours') is informal and unquantified.

Presentation quality is below the bar for a top venue: repeated typos ('pedestrain', 'diversifys', 'protocals', 'robustenss'), a truncated abstract ('will be released a'), an incomplete Table 5 referenced as full in the appendix, and Eq. (9)-(10)/(14)-(16) duplicating content between main text and appendix. There is also no discussion of ethics/privacy beyond a blanket statement, despite collecting surveillance and traffic-camera footage of bystanders.

Novelty positioning is questionable: scene/dataset-dependent definitions (Cao et al., Cho et al.) and text-conditioned VAD overlap substantially with the proposal, and the paper does not clearly delineate what is new beyond combining a text-conditioned head, a contrastive loss, and a data-concatenation augmentation, each of which is individually a known technique.

strengths: The paper identifies a genuinely relevant and under-explored problem: concept drift (changing anomaly definitions) in video anomaly detection, and the formalization of conditioning detection on both video V and anomaly definition Z (Eq. 2-4) is clean and provides a clear reframing that unifies closed-set, open-set, and open-vocabulary methods under one view.

Two substantial contributions rather than one: a new paradigm/model (LaGoVAD) and a large-scale, newly curated dataset (PreVAD, 35,279 videos with hierarchical taxonomy and anomaly descriptions), with a well-documented, scalable human-AI curation pipeline including explicit prompts (Sec. C), which supports reproducibility.

Evaluation is unusually broad for this area: zero-shot cross-domain evaluation on seven test datasets (Protocol 1) plus a dedicated concept-drift protocol (drift@5, Protocol 2), with comparisons against weakly-supervised, zero-shot, open-vocabulary, domain-generalization, and LLM-based methods.

The ablations are reasonably thorough: component-wise ablations (Tab. 5/F), hyperparameter sweeps for dynamic video synthesis (Tab. D), prompting ablations (Tab. E), data-usage scaling (Fig. E), and qualitative visualizations of score curves under concept drift (Fig. 4).

Importantly, the authors include a control where VadCLIP is retrained on PreVAD (Tab. 2), which partially disentangles the gains attributable to the dataset versus the proposed model (7.2% average detection gain from LaGoVAD over VadCLIP on the same data).
weaknesses: Potential data contamination threatens the central zero-shot claims: PreVAD draws 57% of its videos from existing video-text datasets (VIDAL-10M, MSR-VTT, VATEX, VALOR) and web collections, and no deduplication audit against the seven test sets is reported. The claim that PreVAD 'obtains videos independently without merging existing VAD datasets' does not rule out near-duplicate videos or overlaps in content between web-sourced training data and web-sourced test data (e.g., UCF-Crime, XD-Violence are also web/movie sourced).

Annotation quality is largely delegated to foundation models (Qwen2-VL for captions/descriptions, Qwen2-72B for abnormality judging) with no reported quantitative label-accuracy audit (e.g., human verification rate on a random sample), so the effective label noise in PreVAD is unknown; descriptions are also LLM-generated from category labels, which may bias the language-conditioned model toward template-like definitions.

Several gains are modest and the comparison fairness is imperfect: in Tab. 2, baselines (PEL, VadCLIP) are trained on single datasets while LaGoVAD uses PreVAD; the strongest evidence is only the VadCLIP-on-PreVAD control. Improvements in Protocol 2 (Tab. 4) over VadCLIP/LAVAD are small (e.g., 0.857 vs 0.813 AUC on XD-drift@5), and no variance/significance is reported for the drift@5 random-subset protocol despite only five random subsets.

The 'manual designed prompts' used as anomaly definitions at inference (Sec. 6.1) constitute a degree of hand-tuning to the test sets' class semantics; the class-name-only ablation (80.44 vs 81.12 AUC) suggests the default configuration is somewhat favorable.

Methodological novelty is moderate: LaGoVAD is essentially a VadCLIP-style pipeline with text conditioning plus two regularization terms (concatenation-based video synthesis and a contrastive loss with hard negatives); both components are individually rather simple, and the technical framing (modeling Z as a stochastic variable) is more conceptual than algorithmic.

Some reported metrics raise questions: extremely low F1 for UCF-Crime classification (16.64) and the reported '88% classification improvement' over VadCLIP-UCF rely on comparing small F1 values; also, minor issues such as inconsistent statements about whether XD data is used at training time (abstract says zero-shot on seven datasets, but Tab. 2 shows 'PreVAD+XD' configurations) could confuse readers.
Some claimed capabilities (fine-grained multi-anomaly classification, practical surveillance use) are only supported by qualitative examples rather than systematic quantitative analysis.
